title: The Roman Republic
description: From the end of the kings to Augustus, read through the people who wrote about it. Each lesson uses one stretch of Roman history to practise a skill from the History course: reading a source for its purpose, weighing a later account, separating cause from condition, and telling change from continuity.
audience: A curious adult who may have done the History course and wants a period to apply it to. They know that Rome had kings, a Republic and emperors, and may have heard of Hannibal and Caesar, but they have not read the ancient writers or asked who wrote each account and why.
outcomes: You'll be able to say what Livy, Polybius, Sallust, Caesar, Plutarch and Augustus each wrote for, and weigh what each can tell us.
You'll be able to tell a founding tradition from evidence for the events it describes.
You'll be able to say which body held which power under the Republic's constitution, and how the Struggle of the Orders changed it.
You'll be able to separate the conditions, causes and trigger of the Second Punic War, and read a casualty figure for who counted it.
You'll be able to compare two explanations of why the Republic broke down and say what each could see from where its writer stood.
You'll be able to put the main events from 509 BCE to 27 BCE in order and work out the intervals between them.
You'll be able to test Augustus's account of his own career against a later account and say what changed and what stayed under his rule.

modules.title: Founding and constitution
modules.summary: What the Romans said about their beginnings, how a Greek observer described the Republic's offices, and how the first written laws came out of a quarrel between the orders.

modules.title: Italy and Carthage
modules.summary: How Rome came to rule Italy, why it went to war with Carthage a second time, and what the accounts of Hannibal's victories can and cannot tell us.

modules.title: Empire and reform
modules.summary: What conquest did to the city and the army, read through writers who disagree about why, with the Gracchi, Marius and Sulla as the cases.

modules.title: The end of the Republic
modules.summary: Catiline, Cicero and the triumvirate, Caesar in his own words and in a later account, and Augustus telling his own story.

lessons.title: Founding stories and what Livy knew
lessons.objective: Tell a founding tradition from evidence for the events it describes, and say what Livy's telling of the early stories is good evidence of.

concepts.title: Tradition
concepts.summary: A story handed down about the past without a record made at the time.

concepts.title: Exemplum
concepts.summary: A story told to show conduct a reader should copy or avoid.

concepts.title: Traditional date
concepts.summary: A date given by later writers for an event that nobody recorded when it happened.

misconceptions: Taking a story as true because a respected historian tells it, when Livy says in his own preface that he will neither affirm nor refute the tales of the founding.
Thinking that a legend is useless as evidence. It cannot show what happened in 509 BCE, but it shows what Romans of Livy's day wanted to believe about the end of the kings.
Treating 753 and 509 BCE as recorded dates. They are the dates Roman tradition gave, and the textbook says so for the first.
sequence: Open on Livy's preface (1A): the tales from before the city was built suit poetry better than history, and he will not affirm or refute them. Ask what a historian is doing when he reports a story he will not vouch for.
Read the wolf story (1B). Livy gives the tale and, beside it, a plain explanation some people offered. Ask how a writer shows that he is passing something on.

Move to the end of the kings and read the Lucretia scene (1C). Ask what the scene is evidence of. It cannot tell us what Sextus Tarquin did, so ask what it tells us about the Roman of the first century BCE who told it.

Set the story beside Livy's own statement of what changed (1D): the consulship became annual, and the consuls kept the kings' powers and signs. A change in how power was held is told as a crime and an oath.

Add what a modern textbook says about the evidence (1E, 1F): a wall on the Palatine, Greek pottery, and a verdict that the expulsion is loosely based on real events, with the date given only as around 500 BCE.
Close on the question the learner can now ask of any founding story: who told it, when, for what, and what could be checked against something else.
examples: Livy writes that tales of the time before the city were closer to poetry than to history and that he will neither affirm nor refute them (1A). He tells them anyway. Telling a story and vouching for it are different acts, and the lesson makes learners say which one Livy is doing at each point.

On the traditional dates, 753 BCE for the founding and 509 BCE for the end of the kings, the kings ruled for 244 years. Livy's summary of Book I names seven kings and gives 38, 40 and 25 years for the last three, which is 103 years; that leaves 141 years for the first four. The pack gives no verdict on whether such long reigns are believable, so the lesson asks the learner what they would want to check and does not answer it.

figures.shows: A timeline from 800 BCE to 400 BCE with two events: the founding of Rome by tradition (753 BCE) and the expulsion of the last king by tradition (509 BCE). Each label says 'by tradition' only after the learner has placed it.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the marker to each event and read its note, then say which of the two dates the textbook gives more cautiously.
figures.placement: The two traditional dates and the gap between them.

figures.shows: Four cards in a row: the wolf story, the Lucretia story, a wall found on the Palatine in 1988, Greek pottery of the same period. Each card shows its source (Livy or the textbook) and a blank 'made when' slot.
figures.learnerAction: Sort the four cards into 'a story told later' and 'something found in the ground', then open each to see who reports it.
figures.placement: Tradition against material evidence.

questionPlan.answer: Treat it as a tradition he reports, not one he vouches for

Treat it as a record he checked against documents
Ignore it, because a legend is worth nothing as evidence

questionPlan.sample: On the traditional dates of 753 BCE for the founding and 509 BCE for the end of the kings, how many years did the kings rule?

questionPlan.answer: A wider context that explains why the change might have happened

A wider context that explains why the change might have happened

questionPlan.sample: What do we call a story handed down about the past without a record made at the time?
questionPlan.answer: tradition

historyNotes: The textbook gives 753 BCE for the founding 'according to Roman tradition' and 509 BCE for the republic (OpenStax lines 17 and 20). The Palatine wall and the Greek pottery are in OpenStax line 29. Livy's dates of birth and death, and the year he began writing, are not in the pack; the textbook says only that he wrote in the first century BCE.

lessons.title: The constitution seen from outside
lessons.objective: Say which body held which power in the middle Republic, and weigh Polybius's description by who he was and what he wanted to explain.

concepts.title: Consul
concepts.summary: One of two magistrates elected each year, in charge of public business at Rome and of the army in the field.

concepts.title: Senate
concepts.summary: The council of former magistrates, which controlled money, foreign relations and advice to the magistrates.

concepts.title: Assembly
concepts.summary: A meeting of citizens that elects magistrates, passes laws and decides on war and peace.

concepts.title: Veto
concepts.summary: A tribune's power to stop an act by saying 'I forbid'.

concepts.title: Mixed constitution
concepts.summary: A system in which monarchic, aristocratic and popular elements check one another, as Polybius describes Rome's.

misconceptions: Calling the consul a ruler with unlimited power. Polybius says that if you look only at the consuls the constitution seems despotic, then shows the consul needs the Senate for supplies and the people for treaties.
Treating Polybius as a neutral reporter. He is a Greek explaining why Rome rose so fast, and he has a thesis: the constitution caused the success.
Assuming every citizen's vote counted the same. The textbook says the Centuriate Assembly gave wealthier citizens more votes (OpenStax line 38).
sequence: Begin with Polybius's purpose (2A): he wants to show how nearly the whole world fell under Rome in somewhat less than fifty-three years. Ask what he would need to show to prove that the constitution was the cause.
Read his central claim (2B): three elements, so balanced that nobody, not even a Roman, could say which kind of government it was.
Take the elements in turn: the consuls (2C), the Senate's grip on money (2D), and what the people decide (2F).
Read how they check one another (2E): the tribunes' veto can stop the Senate from even meeting, so the Senate must take the people into account.
Sort powers among the bodies, then ask which of Polybius's claims the learner could test against another source, such as the textbook's account of the assemblies.
Weigh the source: an outsider writing for Greek readers, explaining a result he already knows, and describing the system at one moment of its history.
examples: A power-sorting task with Polybius's own list: command the legions on campaign (consuls), spend public money (Senate, through the treasury), ratify a treaty (people), stop the Senate meeting (a tribune's veto), and decide whether to go to war (people, 2F).

Polybius says Rome came under its power in somewhat less than fifty-three years (2A). The pack does not give the start and end years, so the lesson asks the learner only to notice that the number is his, chosen to make the point that the rise was fast.

figures.shows: Three circles labelled Consuls, Senate, People, with arrows between them. Each arrow carries a blank label.
figures.learnerAction: Click each arrow and choose what one body needs from the other (supplies, a decree, a vote, a veto) from a short list, then check against Polybius's text.
figures.placement: How the three check one another.

figures.shows: Rows for six powers (command in the field, spend public money, declare war, pass a law, try a capital case, stop the Senate meeting) and columns for the three bodies and the tribunes.
figures.learnerAction: Tick the body that held each power in Polybius's account; the table marks any row where the learner chose the body that only looks as if it held it.
figures.placement: Assigning powers.

questionPlan.sample: In Polybius's account, which body controlled the spending of public money?
questionPlan.answer: The Senate
choices: The Senate
The consuls
The assembly of the people

questionPlan.sample: What is the word for a tribune stopping an act by saying 'I forbid'?
questionPlan.answer: veto

questionPlan.sample: Polybius was a Greek writing about Rome. Which is the best reason to check his account of the Senate against another source?
questionPlan.answer: He is explaining why Rome won, so he has a reason to find the system well balanced
choices: He could not read Latin, so he invented the details
He is explaining why Rome won, so he has a reason to find the system well balanced
Greek writers never described Roman institutions accurately

questionPlan.sample: Polybius says Rome came under its power in somewhat less than how many years? Give the number in his sentence.
Polybius says that looking only at the consuls would make the constitution seem despotic. What does he conclude from that?
questionPlan.answer: Each part looks like a different system until you see how the others check it
choices: Rome was a monarchy in all but name
The consuls could overrule the Senate and the people
Each part looks like a different system until you see how the others check it

historyNotes: The translator's marginal note places the description at the time of Cannae, 216 BCE; that note is the translator's, not Polybius's. Polybius's own dates of birth and death and his time as a hostage in Rome are not in the pack. The assemblies, the tribunes' veto and the wealth-weighted votes are in OpenStax lines 34 to 39.

lessons.title: The Struggle of the Orders and the Twelve Tables
lessons.objective: Use a narrative and a law code together to say what changed and what stayed the same in the early Republic, and what each is evidence of.

concepts.title: The two orders
concepts.summary: Patricians, the old governing families, and plebeians, the other citizens, who for generations could not hold the main offices.

concepts.title: Secession
concepts.summary: A refusal by the plebeians to serve or to stay in the city until their demands were met.

concepts.title: The Twelve Tables
concepts.summary: Rome's first written laws, traditionally dated to about 450 BCE.

concepts.title: Change and continuity
concepts.summary: What a period altered and what it left as it was; both need evidence.

misconceptions: Reading a law as a picture of what people did. A rule shows what someone wanted allowed or forbidden, not how often it happened.
Treating the Struggle as rich against poor. The textbook says it gave well-off plebeians access to power, and that it did not bring equality to everyone (OpenStax line 35).

Taking Livy's scene of the debtor as an eyewitness account. Livy wrote more than four centuries after the events he describes, so his scene shows what a later Roman thought a debtor's grievance looked like.
sequence: Put two texts on the same problem side by side: Livy's old soldier showing his scarred back to the crowd (3A) and the clause of the Tables that says what a creditor may do (3D).
Read how the dispute ended (3B): two tribunes, then more, with Livy noting that his sources disagree about how many were first chosen.
Read Livy on the ten tables (3C) and his claim that they are still the source of Roman law in his own day.
Read what the Tables say about debt, marriage and the people's last decision (3D, 3E) and about bribed judges and killing an unconvicted man (3F).
Ask what changed: laws written down and open to all. Ask what stayed: debt bondage, a bar on marriage between the orders.
Place the later steps on a line (367 BCE, 287 BCE) and ask which of them changed the clauses the learner has just read.
examples: Table III gives a debtor thirty days after judgment. After that the creditor may bring him before the magistrate and fasten him with not less than fifteen pounds of weight, and if the prisoner will not feed himself the creditor must give a pound of meal a day (3D). The clause shows what the law allowed; the debtor's scene in Livy shows how a later writer pictured the harm.
From the law that one consul must be a plebeian (367 BCE) to the law that assembly decisions of the plebeians bind all citizens (287 BCE) is 80 years (OpenStax line 35).

figures.shows: A timeline from 509 BCE to 250 BCE with the first secession (by Livy's order of events, undated in the pack), the Twelve Tables (about 450 BCE), the plebeian consul (367 BCE) and plebeian assembly laws binding all (287 BCE).
figures.learnerAction: Place each step, then read what the step changed.
figures.placement: The sequence of the Struggle.

figures.shows: Two columns, 'Livy's story' and 'The clause', with rows for debt, the tribunes and marriage. The right column is hidden until the learner says what the left column can and cannot show.
figures.learnerAction: Fill the 'what this is evidence of' cell for each row from three options.
figures.placement: Narrative and law as different kinds of evidence.

questionPlan.sample: Table III lets a creditor hold a debtor in fetters, and Livy tells of a veteran showing the marks of his chains. What is the best use of the two together?
questionPlan.answer: The law shows what was allowed; Livy's scene shows how a later Roman pictured the harm
choices: The law shows what was allowed; Livy's scene shows how a later Roman pictured the harm
Livy's scene proves the law was always applied
The law is the only reliable one of the two, so the scene can be ignored

questionPlan.sample: The plebeian consul was required from 367 BCE and assembly laws of the plebeians bound all citizens from 287 BCE. How many years is that?
Put in order: the Twelve Tables are written down; one consul must be a plebeian; plebeian assembly laws bind all citizens; the plebeians withdraw to the sacred mount (as Livy tells it).
questionPlan.answer: Plebeians withdraw to the sacred mount; Twelve Tables; plebeian consul (367 BCE); plebeian assembly laws bind all (287 BCE)

questionPlan.sample: Table XI bars marriage between plebeians and patricians. What is that clause best evidence of?
questionPlan.answer: That when the Tables were written, the two orders were treated as legally apart
choices: That no plebeian had ever married a patrician
That when the Tables were written, the two orders were treated as legally apart
That the ban was never changed

historyNotes: The Fordham text is Thatcher's 1901 translation, modernised, and gives only fragments, so clause numbers follow that edition. The traditional date of the first secession is not in the pack. OpenStax line 31 says the plebeians struck for the first time in 450 BCE and line 34 says the tribunes were elected 'after 450 BCE'; Livy puts the first tribunes earlier, after the first secession, and says ten were first elected thirty-six years after the first tribunes (Livy lines 7158 to 7160). Do not set Livy against the textbook as fact without an outside check.

lessons.title: How Rome came to rule Italy
lessons.objective: Explain Roman expansion in Italy as a mix of conditions and policies with no master plan, and say what each source can and cannot show about it.

concepts.title: Ally
concepts.summary: A self-governing Italian community tied to Rome by treaty, which sent troops when the consuls asked.

concepts.title: Citizen levy
concepts.summary: An army raised each year from citizens who own property, rather than hired soldiers.

concepts.title: Colony
concepts.summary: A settlement of Roman citizens planted in conquered land, joined to Rome by roads.

misconceptions: Assuming Rome planned to conquer Italy. The textbook says the early Romans did not plan on building an immense empire (4A).
Explaining Rome's success by fighting skill alone. Polybius gives the citizen levy and the allies; the textbook gives colonies, roads and the treatment of beaten enemies.
Using Livy's story of Romulus and the neighbouring cities as evidence of a policy in the 700s BCE. It is a later picture of how Rome grew.
sequence: Open with a question: why Rome and not another Italian city? Read the textbook's answer that Rome did not plan an empire (4A).
Read the list of methods (4B) and the treatment of beaten enemies (4C), and ask which are conditions and which are choices.
Go inside the army with Polybius (4D): the consuls send orders to allied cities, which enrol troops with the same ceremonies.
Read why Rome could keep fighting after defeats (4E): citizens and allies rather than mercenaries.
Read Livy's story of Romulus asking neighbours for marriage rights (4F) and ask what it is evidence of.
Sort the factors into conditions, policies and chances, and say where the pack gives no evidence at all.
examples: Polybius says the first division of the forces raised is into four legions, each of 4,200 infantry and 300 horse, or 5,000 infantry in times of special danger. Four ordinary legions are 4 x (4,200 + 300) = 18,000 men (Polybius lines 630 and 651 to 656).
A source pair: the textbook (4B, a modern summary) and Polybius (4E, an ancient writer describing the system at work). The question is which of them can be checked against the other.

figures.shows: A schematic, not a map: Rome at the centre, a ring of colonies joined by lines (roads), and an outer ring of allied cities, each sending a block of troops to the centre. Labels are hidden until chosen.
figures.learnerAction: Tap each ring to see what Rome asked of it and what it received.
figures.placement: The system of colonies and allies.

figures.shows: Three columns: Condition, Policy, Chance. Six factors to place: hostile neighbours, divide and conquer, colonies on conquered land, a citizen levy, roads, self-government for allies.
figures.learnerAction: Drag each factor to a column; the table marks any the learner places as chance but which the textbook says Rome chose.
figures.placement: Separating what Rome faced from what Rome did.

questionPlan.sample: Polybius divides the forces raised into four legions of 4,200 infantry and 300 horse each. How many men are in the four legions?
The textbook says Rome planted colonies in conquered land and linked them by roads. In the lesson's terms, that is best classed as:
questionPlan.answer: A policy
choices: A condition
A chance event
A policy

questionPlan.sample: Polybius gives the citizen levy as a reason Rome kept fighting after defeats. Which source could most easily check that claim against how the system was built?
questionPlan.answer: His own description of the levy and of the allied contingents in the same book
choices: His own description of the levy and of the allied contingents in the same book
Livy's story of Romulus
A modern map of the roads

questionPlan.sample: Livy has Romulus asking neighbouring cities for marriage rights. What is that story best evidence of?
questionPlan.answer: How a Roman of Livy's day pictured Rome growing by joining others
choices: A treaty policy in the 700s BCE
How a Roman of Livy's day pictured Rome growing by joining others
The date the first colony was planted

historyNotes: The pack has no narrative of the Latin, Samnite or Pyrrhic wars: Livy Books 4 to 20 are not in it. The lesson therefore teaches the system and its causes, not a campaign history, and its dates come from the textbook (the First Punic War begins in 264 BCE).

lessons.title: Why the Second Punic War began
lessons.objective: Separate the conditions, causes and trigger of the Second Punic War, and show where Livy's account takes Rome's side.

concepts.title: Hedged report
concepts.summary: A claim a writer passes on while signalling that he does not vouch for it, with words such as 'there is a story' or 'it is said'.

concepts.title: Partisan source
concepts.summary: A source written by someone on one side of the matter it describes.

concepts.title: War guilt
concepts.summary: The question of which side is to blame for starting a war.

misconceptions: Taking Livy's oath scene as a cause of the war. Livy introduces it with 'there is besides a story' (5C).
Treating the attack on Saguntum as the whole cause. Livy himself reports resentment over Sicily and Sardinia and a dispute about which treaty bound whom.
Treating praise of one's own side as neutral. Livy says the Roman way of declaring war was more consistent with Rome's dignity than arguing about treaties (5F).
sequence: Open with the textbook's outline (5A): the First Punic War from 264 to 241 BCE, and the Second from 218 BCE. Ask what Carthage and Rome each wanted.
Read Livy's opening (5B): the hatred on both sides was almost greater than their resources, and he says why for each.
Read the oath story and the lost islands (5C). Ask which is a story and which is a grievance, and what Livy's wording tells us.
Read Livy on Hannibal's plan (5D): the claim is about intention. Ask who could have known it.
Read the treaty argument and the declaration of war (5E), then Livy's own verdict (5F).
Sort the factors into condition, cause and trigger, and defend one placement against Livy's account.
examples: The First Punic War ran from 264 to 241 BCE and the Second began in 218 BCE. The gap between them is 241 minus 218, which is 23 years (OpenStax lines 46 and 47).

A sort for the lesson: Carthage's resentment of the loss of Sicily and Sardinia and the tribute (condition); Hannibal's decision to attack Saguntum, as Livy reports it (cause); the fall of Saguntum and the Roman embassy's declaration (trigger).

figures.shows: A timeline from 270 BCE to 200 BCE with the First Punic War (264 to 241), the start of the Second (218) and the Battle of Zama (202), each with a short note.
figures.learnerAction: Place the three markers and read the gap between the wars.
figures.placement: The long gap between the two wars.

figures.shows: Three columns: Condition, Cause, Trigger. Cards with Livy's page references.
figures.learnerAction: Place each card, then open Livy's wording to see which words support the placement.
figures.placement: Applying the History lesson on causes.

questionPlan.sample: The First Punic War ended in 241 BCE and the Second began in 218 BCE. How many years passed between them?
Livy introduces Hannibal's boyhood oath with 'there is besides a story'. How should a historian treat the oath?
questionPlan.answer: As a story Livy passes on without vouching for it
choices: As a record of what Hannibal swore
As proof that Carthage wanted war from 237 BCE
As a story Livy passes on without vouching for it

questionPlan.sample: Hamilcar's anger at the loss of Sicily and Sardinia is best classed, in Livy's account, as:
questionPlan.answer: A condition
choices: A condition
The trigger
A modern invention

questionPlan.sample: Which of Livy's remarks shows him taking the Roman side?
questionPlan.answer: That the Roman declaration of war was more consistent with Rome's dignity than arguing about treaties
choices: That Hannibal was a skilful general
That the Roman declaration of war was more consistent with Rome's dignity than arguing about treaties
That the hatred on both sides was almost greater than their resources

questionPlan.sample: The Carthaginian envoy's speech about the treaties appears in Livy. A careful reader treats it as:
questionPlan.answer: Livy's version of the Carthaginian case, written by a Roman
choices: A Carthaginian record copied word for word
A forgery added later
Livy's version of the Carthaginian case, written by a Roman

historyNotes: Dates: First Punic War 264 to 241 BCE, Second 218 to 201 BCE, Zama 202 BCE (OpenStax lines 46 to 49). Livy's own discussion of which year Saguntum fell and which consuls held office is at Livy lines 9640 to 9651 and shows that even he was unsure of the sequence. Polybius's judgment that Carthage was past its prime by the time of the war is at Polybius lines 1596 to 1617.

lessons.title: Hannibal in Italy and the numbers at Cannae
lessons.objective: Read a casualty figure in an ancient source for who counted it and how sure the writer is, and compare two accounts of what Cannae did to Rome's allies.

concepts.title: Hedged number
concepts.summary: A figure given with a sign that the writer cannot vouch for it, such as 'are said to have been'.

concepts.title: Authority
concepts.summary: The earlier writer a historian names as the source of a claim.

concepts.title: Corroboration
concepts.summary: Support for a claim from a second source that did not get it from the first.

misconceptions: Reading 'forty thousand foot' as a count. Livy writes that the dead 'are said to have been' that many.
Taking the famous exchange with Maharbal as a record of what was said. Nobody on the Roman side could have heard it, and Livy writes that the delay is 'firmly believed' to have saved the city.
Assuming a great defeat ends a war. Polybius and the textbook differ on how many allies Rome kept after Cannae, and the lesson makes learners ask what each means by 'allies'.
sequence: Read Livy on Trasimene (6B): he gives numbers for both sides and says he follows Fabius, a contemporary, over writers who give far larger figures.
Read Livy's figures for Cannae (6C) and total them. Ask which words in the sentence tell us how sure he is.
Read Maharbal and the delay (6D). Ask who could have told Livy what was said in Hannibal's tent.
Read Polybius on the Senate's refusal to ransom the prisoners (6A, 6E): the claim about allies, and the lesson the refusal taught Roman soldiers.
Put Polybius's claim beside the textbook's (6F). Ask what each could mean by 'allies' and who is closer in time.
Order the battles and note what the pack does and does not date.
examples: Livy: forty thousand foot and two thousand seven hundred horse, an equal number of citizens and allies, are said to have been slain at Cannae (6C). Together that is 42,700, and with an equal split about 21,350 citizens and 21,350 allies.
At Trasimene Livy gives 15,000 Romans slain and 1,500 of the enemy, a ratio of 10 to 1 (6B), and says that some authors record far more (6B).

figures.shows: Two horizontal bars for the Trasimene figures and two for Cannae, each with a label on the word that hedges the figure. The label text is hidden until the learner chooses which word hedges it.
figures.learnerAction: Tap the word in each sentence that shows how sure Livy is.
figures.placement: Where a number comes from.

figures.shows: Four battle cards (Trebia, Trasimene, Cannae, Zama) with no dates visible.
figures.learnerAction: Put the four in order using Livy's book order and the textbook.
figures.placement: Sequence of the war.

questionPlan.sample: Livy says forty thousand foot and two thousand seven hundred horse 'are said to have been slain' at Cannae. What is the total?
Which words in Livy's sentence about Cannae show he is not sure of the count?
questionPlan.answer: 'are said to have been slain'
choices: 'are said to have been slain'
'forty thousand foot'
'an equal number of citizens and allies'

questionPlan.sample: Source A (Polybius) says that after Cannae Rome was roughly deprived of all its allies. Source B (a textbook) says most of the Italian allies stayed loyal. What is the best first step?
questionPlan.answer: Ask what each means by 'allies' and when it is describing
choices: Trust the newer one
Ask what each means by 'allies' and when it is describing
Average the two

questionPlan.sample: Livy gives Maharbal's remark that Hannibal knew how to win but not how to use a victory. Why is that remark weak evidence of what was said?
questionPlan.answer: No Roman was present, and Livy writes only that the delay is believed to have saved the city
choices: Livy had no interest in Hannibal
Maharbal was never a real person
No Roman was present, and Livy writes only that the delay is believed to have saved the city

questionPlan.sample: Put in order: Zama; Cannae; the Trebia; Trasimene.
questionPlan.answer: The Trebia; Trasimene; Cannae; Zama

historyNotes: The translator's marginal note dates Cannae to 216 BCE; the textbook dates Zama to 202 BCE (OpenStax line 49). Dates for the Trebia (218) and Trasimene (217) are not in the pack and need checking before they are shown. Polybius gives 'three minae' as the ransom Hannibal asked; Livy gives 300 denarii for a Roman citizen, 200 for an ally and 100 for a slave (Livy lines 13570 to 13572). Whether the two sums are the same is not settled by the pack.

lessons.title: What empire did to Rome
lessons.objective: Compare three explanations of the Republic's troubles, say which parts are fact, evidence or interpretation, and say what each writer could see from where he stood.

concepts.title: Moral explanation
concepts.summary: An explanation of events by the habits and character of a people or its leaders.

concepts.title: Proletariat
concepts.summary: The landless working poor of the city of Rome, as the textbook uses the word.

concepts.title: Interpretation
concepts.summary: An account that selects facts and weighs them to explain what happened.

misconceptions: Treating Sallust's claim that fear of Carthage kept Rome in order as a fact. It is a judgement about people's minds, and he offers no test of it.
Setting Polybius on bribery (death for it at Rome) against Sallust's 'a city for sale' as a plain before and after. They are different writers, with different aims, describing different moments.
Thinking that explanations by morals are modern. Polybius predicted this kind of decline in his own day (7F).
sequence: Begin with Polybius at the height of Rome's power (7A): he says bribery for office is punished by death at Rome and is open at Carthage.
Read Sallust on Jugurtha leaving Rome (7B): the city could be bought if a purchaser appeared. Ask whether this contradicts Polybius.
Read Sallust's cause (7C, 7D): fear of Carthage held the state together, and wealth and security after its fall began the rot.
Read the textbook's cause (7E): long wars, farms left empty, the landless in the city.
Read Polybius's forecast (7F): how great wealth and rivalry for office lead to mob-rule.
Sort statements into fact, evidence and interpretation, then ask what would test each explanation.
examples: The textbook dates the destruction of Carthage and the sack of Corinth to 146 BCE and the war with Jugurtha to 112 BCE (OpenStax lines 53 and 66). The gap is 146 minus 112, which is 34 years. Sallust's explanation puts the change in the years after 146 BCE, so the war with Jugurtha is about a generation on.

The textbook says that after the defeat of Perseus in 168 BCE the Romans enslaved 150,000 people from Epirus and that Delos reportedly sold ten thousand people a day (OpenStax line 59). The 'reportedly' is the textbook's. A learner is asked how the figures could have been counted.

figures.shows: A timeline from 220 BCE to 100 BCE with four markers: Polybius's Rome at its height (216 BCE), the sack of Corinth and Carthage (146 BCE), the war with Jugurtha (112 BCE), and the point where Sallust says the change began (after 146 BCE).
figures.learnerAction: Place each marker, then say which of Polybius and Sallust is describing which moment.
figures.placement: Different writers, different moments.

figures.shows: Three columns, Polybius, Sallust and the textbook, with rows for what each says went wrong and what evidence is given.
figures.learnerAction: Fill the 'evidence given' cell for each; the table marks any cell left blank because the source gives none.
figures.placement: Comparing explanations.

questionPlan.sample: Carthage and Corinth were destroyed in 146 BCE and the war with Jugurtha began in 112 BCE. How many years is that?
Sallust writes that before Carthage was destroyed the dread of an enemy kept the state in order. What kind of claim is that?
questionPlan.answer: An interpretation
choices: An interpretation
A fact
A piece of evidence

questionPlan.sample: Source A is Polybius saying the Romans punish bribery for office with death. Source B is Sallust's report that Jugurtha called Rome a city for sale. What is the best conclusion?
questionPlan.answer: They were written at different times by writers with different aims, so they cannot just be set side by side as before and after
choices: Polybius was lying
They were written at different times by writers with different aims, so they cannot just be set side by side as before and after
Sallust proves bribery was unknown in Polybius's day

questionPlan.sample: The textbook says Delos 'reportedly' sold ten thousand people a day. What does 'reportedly' tell a careful reader?
questionPlan.answer: The figure is passed on without a count behind it
choices: The figure was counted at the time
The figure is certainly wrong
The figure is passed on without a count behind it

questionPlan.sample: Rate how well you could say, for each of Polybius, Sallust and the textbook, what the writer thinks went wrong with Rome and what the writer offers as evidence.
questionPlan.answer: Self-rated 1 to 5

historyNotes: Sallust's own dates, and the dates when he wrote the two monographs, are not in the pack. The year of the Jugurthine war (112 BCE) and of the destruction of Carthage and Corinth (146 BCE) come from the textbook. Polybius's account of Rome at its height is set, by the translator's note, at 216 BCE.

lessons.title: The Gracchi and a later biographer
lessons.objective: Weigh what a biographer writing long after the events can know about motives, by tracing who each claim comes from and comparing a second account.

concepts.title: Later account
concepts.summary: An account written long after the events, built on earlier sources, some of which it names.

concepts.title: Chain of testimony
concepts.summary: The line from an event to the reader: who saw it, who told whom, who wrote it down.

concepts.title: Tribune
concepts.summary: An official elected by the plebeians who could propose laws and stop the acts of others.

misconceptions: Assuming a vivid scene came from an eyewitness. Plutarch names Caius Gracchus's writing for one claim and says 'we are told' for another.
Taking a reported speech as the speaker's words. Plutarch gives Tiberius a speech that the pack cannot check.
Reading Plutarch's sympathy for the Gracchi as the whole picture. Sallust, writing from the other side, blames the Gracchi for lack of prudence as well as the nobility for violence.
sequence: Open on the problem as Plutarch states it (8A): earlier limits on land were evaded, free farmers replaced by slaves, and the textbook's account agrees in outline.
Read Plutarch's list of motives for Tiberius's law (8B) and ask who each claim is attributed to.
Read the claim he sources to Caius Gracchus himself (8C) and the public notices urging Tiberius on. Ask what it means to rely on the brother's testimony.
Read Tiberius's reason for asking the people to remove a fellow tribune (8D), then Plutarch's remark on the first bloodshed (8E).
Read Sallust on the Gracchi (8F). Ask what he and Plutarch agree on and where their verdicts differ.
Close on a short checklist for a later account: who is named, who is not, what could be checked, and what the writer wants.
examples: Plutarch lists several explanations for Tiberius's law: advice from a rhetorician and a philosopher, his mother's reproaches, a rivalry with Spurius Postumius, and his brother Caius's own writing that he saw an empty countryside on his way to Numantia (8B, 8C). He says it is also 'most certain' that public notices urged him on. That is five claims, each introduced differently ('most commonly stated', 'some have charged', 'others say', 'in writing', 'most certain'), and the learner is asked to rank them by how close each claim could be to Tiberius.
Tiberius's law is dated to 133 BCE and Gaius's death to 121 BCE (OpenStax lines 63 and 64), a gap of 12 years.

figures.shows: A chain of boxes from 'Tiberius in 133 BCE' to 'a reader today', with Caius Gracchus's writing, other authors Plutarch names, Plutarch, and the translator as links. Each link has a blank 'when' slot.
figures.learnerAction: Click each link to open the passage that shows it, and mark any link the pack cannot confirm.
figures.placement: Following a claim back to its source.

figures.shows: Rows for each motive Plutarch lists; columns 'Who said so', 'Close to Tiberius?', 'Could he know?'.
figures.learnerAction: Fill the second and third columns from the passage.
figures.placement: Weighing claims by their source.

questionPlan.sample: Plutarch says Caius Gracchus wrote that Tiberius first conceived his policy on seeing the empty countryside on the way to Numantia. What does that make the claim?
questionPlan.answer: A claim from the brother of the man, passed on at second hand
choices: A claim from the brother of the man, passed on at second hand
An eyewitness record of Tiberius's reasons
A rumour with no source

questionPlan.sample: Tiberius's land law is dated to 133 BCE and Gaius died in 121 BCE. How many years is that?
Source A is Plutarch on the death of Tiberius. Source B is Sallust on the Gracchi. Which statement do both support?
questionPlan.answer: Senators and their allies killed Tiberius
choices: Tiberius had no support among the people
Senators and their allies killed Tiberius
Tiberius planned to make himself king

questionPlan.sample: Plutarch gives Tiberius a speech about the beasts of Italy having dens while soldiers have only air and light. How should a historian use it?
questionPlan.answer: As Plutarch's version of the argument, not Tiberius's exact words
choices: As Tiberius's exact words
Not at all, because speeches in histories are always invented
As Plutarch's version of the argument, not Tiberius's exact words

questionPlan.sample: Rate your recall: name the questions to ask of a later account and say which of them the Plutarch passages answer.
questionPlan.answer: Self-rated 1 to 5

historyNotes: Plutarch's dates of birth and death, and the century he wrote in, are not in the pack. The textbook calls the Gracchi grandsons of Scipio Africanus (OpenStax line 63). Gaius was tribune 'ten years later' than Tiberius by the textbook; the year is not given. Plutarch's own statement that three hundred died by clubs and staves and 'none by an iron weapon' is at Plutarch lines 9515 to 9517.

lessons.title: Marius, Sulla and soldiers who followed a general
lessons.objective: Explain how soldiers' loyalty moved from the state to their commanders, separating what Sallust and Plutarch report from what the textbook concludes.

concepts.title: Client army
concepts.summary: An army whose soldiers are more loyal to their commander, who promises them pay and land, than to the state.

concepts.title: Proscription
concepts.summary: A published list of men whom anyone might kill, and whose property was seized.

concepts.title: Dictator
concepts.summary: An old office that gave absolute authority for a limited time to meet an emergency.

misconceptions: Crediting Marius alone with changing the army. Sallust gives two explanations for his enlistment of the poor and does not choose between them.
Reading Marius's speech as a record of his words. Sallust composed it, and it shows Sallust's picture of the man.
Treating Sulla's dictatorship as the old office again. Plutarch says it had been laid aside for 120 years and that the powers voted were far wider than an emergency.
sequence: Begin with Sallust's account of the enlistment (9A): he took all who would come, mostly from the lowest ranks, and Sallust gives two reasons without choosing.
Read part of the speech Sallust gives Marius (9B). Ask what Marius is claiming about nobility, and whose picture of him it is.
Read the textbook's summary (9C) and compare how sure it is with how sure Sallust is.
Read Plutarch on the march on Rome (9D), then the proscriptions (9E) and the dictatorship (9F).
Order the stages and place each stage as change or continuity from what Polybius described.
Ask the central question: was the new thing the soldiers, the commanders' promises, or the willingness to use the army inside Italy?
examples: Plutarch says Sulla proscribed eighty names, then two hundred and twenty more after one day's wait, and 'on the third again, as many' (9E). Reading 'as many' as 220, the total is 80 + 220 + 220 = 520.

Plutarch says the office of dictator had been laid aside for 120 years (9F). The textbook says it had not been used since the Second Punic War, which ended in 201 BCE (OpenStax lines 72 and 47). 120 years before Sulla's dictatorship in 82 BCE is 202 BCE, so the two accounts agree.

figures.shows: A timeline from 115 BCE to 75 BCE with Marius elected consul promising to end the Jugurthine war (107), Sulla marches on Rome (88), Marius marches on Rome (87), Sulla resigns (79).
figures.learnerAction: Place each event and read the note.
figures.placement: Stages of the break between army and state.

figures.shows: Two columns, 'What Sallust or Plutarch says' and 'What the textbook says', for the enlistment, the march on Rome and the dictatorship.
figures.learnerAction: Fill the last row from the passages; the table highlights where the textbook is more certain than Sallust.
figures.placement: Comparing a primary source and a summary.

questionPlan.sample: Plutarch says Sulla proscribed eighty persons, then two hundred and twenty more, and on the third day 'as many' as the second. How many names in all?
Sallust says Marius enlisted the poor because better men were scarce, or because he wanted to court the poor who had honoured him. How should a historian record these?
questionPlan.answer: As two explanations Sallust reports without choosing
choices: As two explanations Sallust reports without choosing
As a proved cause
As an invention of Marius's enemies

questionPlan.sample: Put in order: Marius elected consul; Sulla marches on Rome; Marius marches on Rome; Sulla gives up the dictatorship.
questionPlan.answer: Marius elected consul (107 BCE); Sulla marches on Rome (88); Marius marches on Rome (87); Sulla gives up the dictatorship (79)

questionPlan.sample: The speech Sallust gives Marius says his scars are his statues and his honours are his nobility. What is it best evidence of?
questionPlan.answer: How Sallust chose to present Marius's case
choices: The exact words Marius used
How Sallust chose to present Marius's case
How many scars Marius had

questionPlan.sample: Plutarch says the dictatorship had been laid aside for 120 years before Sulla took it. What does that point to?
questionPlan.answer: Change: an emergency office used as a long-term rule
choices: Continuity: the Romans used dictators often
Nothing, because the number is invented
Change: an emergency office used as a long-term rule

historyNotes: The textbook gives 107 BCE for Marius's election, 88 for Sulla's march, 87 for Marius's march, 83 for Sulla's return and 79 for his resignation (OpenStax lines 67 to 73). It does not give the year he became dictator; 82 BCE comes from outside the pack and must be checked. The textbook's 'five consecutive terms (105 to 101 BCE)' for Marius looks a year off from other lists and should not be used for a date question.

lessons.title: Catiline, Cicero and the first triumvirate
lessons.objective: Read Sallust's account of Catiline for its author's purpose, check it against Plutarch, and say how Plutarch explains the road to civil war.

concepts.title: Conspiracy
concepts.summary: A secret plan by a group to seize power or overthrow the government.

concepts.title: Triumvirate
concepts.summary: A private alliance of three men; the first, in 60 BCE, joined Pompey, Crassus and Caesar.

concepts.title: Claimed impartiality
concepts.summary: A writer's statement that he has no interest in the matter, which is itself something he chose to say.

misconceptions: Taking Sallust's claim to write without hope, fear or party interest (10A) as a fact about his book. It is a claim, and a historian checks it against what he writes.
Counting two accounts that agree as two independent witnesses. The pack does not say whether Plutarch used Sallust or a common source.
Treating the First Triumvirate as a quarrel that broke into war. Plutarch says the civil wars began from their union, not their quarrel (10D).
sequence: Begin with what Sallust says about himself and his book (10A). Ask what he wants the reader to believe about his motives.
Read how Sallust handles a rumour about Caesar (10B). Ask whose side the sentence favours.
Read Plutarch on the Senate's debate (10C) and set it beside Sallust: both report that suspicion fell on Caesar.
Read Plutarch on the alliance of Pompey, Crassus and Caesar (10D) and ask what kind of claim it is.
Read Polybius on the people as the court of life and death (10E) and Plutarch on the charge later brought against Cicero (10F). Ask what rule Cicero's critics said was broken.
Close on the skill: purpose, corroboration, and a cause claim to be tested.
examples: The textbook dates the triumvirate to 60 BCE and Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon to January 49 BCE (OpenStax lines 88 and 89), so the alliance lasted 60 minus 49 = 11 years before the war it is said to have caused began.

Plutarch writes that Cicero was charged, after his consulship, with putting citizens to death without a trial (10F). Table IX forbids putting an unconvicted man to death (3F) and Polybius says the people were the only court for capital cases (10E). The three are three kinds of evidence about one rule: a law, a description, and an accusation.

figures.shows: Two columns for 'Sallust' and 'Plutarch', with rows for what each says about Catiline, the Senate's debate and Caesar. Cells where both say the same are left empty until the learner chooses to reveal them.
figures.learnerAction: Mark each row as 'agree', 'differ' or 'only one says it'.
figures.placement: Corroboration across two sources.

figures.shows: Five cards: the triumvirate is formed, Crassus dies, Caesar crosses the Rubicon, Pharsalus, the assassination.
figures.learnerAction: Put in order.
figures.placement: Ties the lesson to the end of the Republic.

questionPlan.sample: Sallust says he writes with a mind 'uninfluenced by hope, fear, or political partisanship'. How should a historian treat that statement?
questionPlan.answer: As a claim to be tested against what the book does
choices: As a claim to be tested against what the book does
As proof the book is neutral
As evidence that he lied

questionPlan.sample: The first triumvirate was made in 60 BCE and Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE. How many years is that?
Source A (Sallust) says enemies of Caesar spread stories that he was in the plot. Source B (Plutarch) says Cato raised strong suspicion about Caesar in the Senate. What do the two together show?
questionPlan.answer: Suspicion of Caesar was part of the debate, though neither proves he was involved
choices: Caesar was certainly in the plot
Suspicion of Caesar was part of the debate, though neither proves he was involved
Neither source mentions Caesar

questionPlan.sample: Plutarch says the civil wars began with the union of Pompey and Caesar, not their quarrel. What would most strengthen that claim?
questionPlan.answer: Evidence of what the alliance did to the Senate's power before the quarrel
choices: A later quarrel between them
Another writer repeating the sentence
Evidence of what the alliance did to the Senate's power before the quarrel

questionPlan.sample: What do we call a writer's own statement that he has no interest in the matter he writes about?
questionPlan.answer: claimed impartiality

historyNotes: The pack does not give the year of the conspiracy or of Cicero's consulship. Sallust names the consuls of 64 BCE (Lucius Caesar and Caius Figulus) when he dates the plot to June, so the year of the plot is argued from that and needs an outside source (Catiline line 430). Sallust's career, his link to Caesar and the dates of his writing are not in the pack. OpenStax line 88 says Caesar was consul in 60 BCE; he was consul in 59, so do not use that sentence for dates.

lessons.title: Caesar in his own words and in Plutarch's
lessons.objective: Read Caesar's own reports for their purpose and compare them with Plutarch's later account, including the scene at the Rubicon.

concepts.title: Commentary
concepts.summary: Caesar's own report of his campaigns, written in the third person for readers at Rome.

concepts.title: Count and census
concepts.summary: A figure Caesar gives from a list or count; the question is who made it.

concepts.title: Justification
concepts.summary: A reason a writer gives for an action, chosen to persuade.

misconceptions: Treating Caesar's third-person reports as detached. He is the general writing about his own war for readers who will judge him.
Thinking the Rubicon scene comes from Caesar. Caesar's Book 1 of the Civil War never names the river; the scene is Plutarch's, who names Asinius Pollio as one of those present.
Comparing two numbers as if they counted the same thing. Caesar's lists are for one migration; Plutarch's totals are for ten years of war.
sequence: Open with Caesar's reason for entering Gaul (11A): the Helvetii would be dangerous neighbours to the Province. Ask who this explanation is for.
Read the lists from the Helvetii camp (11B) and total them. Ask who made the lists and who reports them.
Set Plutarch's totals for the whole of the Gallic wars (11C) beside Caesar's single count.
Read Caesar's speech to his soldiers at the start of the civil war (11D). Ask what precedents he uses and why.
Read Plutarch's Rubicon (11E, 11F). Ask where the scene could come from and what Plutarch says himself.
Weigh the two: each is useful, for different questions.
examples: Caesar reports lists found in the camp of the Helvetii: 263,000 Helvetii, 36,000 Tulingi, 14,000 Latobrigi, 23,000 Rauraci and 32,000 Boii, 368,000 in all, of whom about 92,000 could bear arms, and he says a census of those who went home found 110,000 (11B). 368,000 minus 110,000 is 258,000 who were not counted at home.

Plutarch says Caesar in under ten years took more than eight hundred towns, subdued three hundred states and fought three million men, of whom one million were killed and a second taken (11C). The figure is for the whole of the Gallic wars and is Plutarch's, not Caesar's.

figures.shows: Two boxes, 'Caesar writes' and 'Plutarch writes', with a blank gap between them labelled with their relationship in time.
figures.learnerAction: Fill in what each knew first-hand and what each had to take from others.
figures.placement: Primary and later account.

figures.shows: Five cards: the triumvirate (60 BCE), Crassus's death (54 BCE), the Rubicon (49 BCE), Pharsalus (48 BCE), the assassination (44 BCE).
figures.learnerAction: Put in order.
figures.placement: Places the lesson on the road to the end of the Republic.

questionPlan.sample: Caesar's lists give 368,000 Helvetii and their allies setting out and 110,000 counted at home. How many are not accounted for at home?
Caesar says he marched into Gaul because the Helvetii would bring danger to the Province. Who is that explanation written for?
questionPlan.answer: Readers at Rome who would judge whether the war was justified
choices: Readers at Rome who would judge whether the war was justified
Soldiers in his camp
Historians writing centuries later

questionPlan.sample: Plutarch has Caesar say 'The die is cast' at the Rubicon and names Asinius Pollio among those with him. What does the name tell a historian?
questionPlan.answer: Where Plutarch says the story may have come from
choices: That Pollio was Plutarch's friend
Where Plutarch says the story may have come from
That Caesar wrote the line down

questionPlan.sample: Why can Caesar's count of the Helvetii not simply be set against Plutarch's totals for the Gallic wars?
questionPlan.answer: They count different things: one migration and ten years of war
choices: One of them must be wrong
Plutarch counted only soldiers
They count different things: one migration and ten years of war

questionPlan.sample: Put in order: Pharsalus; the first triumvirate; the crossing of the Rubicon; Crassus's death.
questionPlan.answer: The first triumvirate (60 BCE); Crassus's death (54 BCE); the Rubicon (49 BCE); Pharsalus (48 BCE)

historyNotes: The textbook dates Crassus's invasion of Parthia to 54 BCE and says he was captured and executed; his death is usually put a year later, so the lesson should use the invasion date only. It dates Pharsalus to 48 BCE, the Rubicon to January 49 BCE and the assassination to 44 BCE (OpenStax lines 88 to 91). When Caesar's commentaries were published is not in the pack. The translation of Gallic War I and Civil War I is McDevitte and Bohn; the pack has Book 1 of each only.

lessons.title: Augustus: the Republic restored, in his own words
lessons.objective: Test Augustus's own account of his career against a later biographer and a textbook, and say what changed and what stayed in the constitution after 27 BCE.

concepts.title: Res Gestae
concepts.summary: Augustus's own list of what he had done, set up on bronze columns in Rome.

concepts.title: Principate
concepts.summary: The system Augustus created, in which a first citizen held power through the old offices.

concepts.title: Facade
concepts.summary: An outward form kept after the substance has changed.

misconceptions: Taking Augustus's list as a neutral record. He wrote it for display, and it says nothing of the proscriptions that Plutarch describes.
Treating the textbook as a check on Augustus when it contradicts him on a point. The textbook says he stepped down as dictator; the Res Gestae says he refused the dictatorship.
Thinking the Republic simply ended. Consuls, the Senate and tribunes continued; the question is who held the real power.
sequence: Open with Augustus's opening claim about himself at nineteen (12A) and what he says he did to the killers of his father (12D).
Read Plutarch on what the three men did together (12E) and note what the Res Gestae leaves out.
Read the refusal of the dictatorship (12B). Ask who might want him to say it.
Read his statement that he handed the republic back to the senate and people, and that after that he held no more power than his colleagues (12C).
Read the textbook's judgement that the restored republic was a facade and that he held tribunician power from 23 BCE (12F).
Sort what changed and what stayed, using Polybius's description from lesson 2 as the baseline.
examples: Augustus counts the thirty-seventh year of his tribunician power at the time of writing (Res Gestae 4). The textbook dates the grant of tribunician powers to 23 BCE (OpenStax line 101). From 23 BCE to 14 CE is 23 + 14 - 1 = 36 years elapsed, so the thirty-seventh year runs into 14 CE, the year of his death (OpenStax line 105).

Augustus says he refused the dictatorship (12B). The textbook says he stepped down as dictator in 27 BCE (12F). Only one of these is likely to be right, and the lesson asks the learner which source is better placed to know and which has a reason to choose its words.

figures.shows: A timeline from 45 BCE to 20 CE with Caesar's assassination (44 BCE), Philippi (42), Actium (31), the settlement of 27 BCE, tribunician power (23 BCE) and Augustus's death (14 CE).
figures.learnerAction: Place each and read the note.
figures.placement: The final stage of the arc.

figures.shows: Two columns, 'Under Polybius's constitution' and 'Under Augustus', with rows for the consuls, the Senate, the assemblies, the tribunes and the army.
figures.learnerAction: Mark each cell 'same', 'changed' or 'kept in name only'.
figures.placement: Change and continuity.

questionPlan.sample: Augustus held tribunician power from 23 BCE and died in 14 CE. How many years is that?
The Res Gestae was set up in public. What does that suggest about how to read it?
questionPlan.answer: As a statement meant to shape how he was remembered
choices: As a statement meant to shape how he was remembered
As a private diary
As a list that any citizen could check

questionPlan.sample: Source A (Plutarch) describes a death list drawn up by the three men and Octavian giving up Cicero. Source B (the Res Gestae) says only that he drove out his father's killers by due process. What does the difference show?
questionPlan.answer: The Res Gestae leaves out what does not fit the story he wants told
choices: Plutarch invented the list
The Res Gestae leaves out what does not fit the story he wants told
Both are complete accounts

questionPlan.sample: After 27 BCE the consuls and the Senate still met, but Augustus held tribunician power and command of the armies. How is that best described?
questionPlan.answer: The old offices continued while the real power moved to one man
choices: The Republic returned unchanged
Everything was abolished
The old offices continued while the real power moved to one man

questionPlan.sample: Rate your recall: name the claim in the Res Gestae that you tested, the source you tested it against, and what you found.
questionPlan.answer: Self-rated 1 to 5

historyNotes: The textbook dates Philippi to 42 BCE, Actium to 31 BCE, the settlement to 27 BCE, tribunician powers to 23 BCE and Augustus's death to 14 CE (OpenStax lines 95 to 105). Res Gestae 35 gives his age as in his seventy-sixth year at the time of writing; his birth date is not in the pack. The textbook says he reduced the army from 600,000 to 200,000 (line 102) while the Res Gestae says about 500,000 citizens took the oath and over 300,000 were settled (chapter 3); the two figures count different things and the lesson should not subtract one from the other.

courseCheck: A mixed set. Source three short extracts for their author, date and purpose. Put a set of events in order and compute intervals across the BCE and CE boundary. Assign six powers to consuls, Senate, assemblies and tribunes. Sort the factors behind the Second Punic War into conditions, causes and trigger. Read two casualty figures and say which words show the writer is unsure. Tell a fact, a piece of evidence and an interpretation apart in a passage of Sallust or Polybius. Compare Plutarch with a primary source on one event and say which can be checked. Set a claim of Augustus beside the textbook and name what would settle it. Finish with a self-rated recall of the questions to ask of any source.
platformNeeds: A source-card figure: an extract with its provenance (author, translator, approximate date, audience, purpose) hidden behind taps, so the learner chooses which question to ask first. Every lesson uses extracts and the fallback is a table plus svg_figure.
A map figure with dated layers for Italy, the western Mediterranean and Hannibal's route (lessons 4, 5, 6). The fallback is a schematic svg_figure.
timeline_explorer must accept BCE years, show five or six events on one axis, and take events with no year (the first secession). The fallback is order_sequence.

A sort question type (cards into two or three bins) for the condition, cause and trigger tasks in lessons 4, 5 and 7, and for the assign-powers task in lesson 2. The curriculum plans each as a series of choice items.

Pair-of-sources extracts with three-part attributions (who, when, kind) for every extract. The pack gives the translator and work but not the dates of the ancient authors; those need adding from outside the pack.
unverified: Dates of the ancient authors, none of which is in the pack: Livy (about 59 BCE to 17 CE, and that he began writing after 27 BCE), Polybius (about 200 to 118 BCE, a hostage at Rome), Sallust (86 to 35 BCE, a supporter of Caesar who left public life), Plutarch (about 46 to 120 CE) and Caesar's dates of writing.
The traditional date of the first secession (494 BCE) and of the tribunes' creation. OpenStax lines 31 and 34 say 450 BCE; Livy places the tribunes earlier.

The Twelve Tables' traditional date of about 450 BCE, and the claim in Spillan's text of 'the three hundred and first year after Rome was built' (Livy line 7245), which may differ from the Latin count.
Dates of the Trebia (218 BCE) and Trasimene (217 BCE), and that Cannae was 2 August 216 BCE. The translator's note gives only 216 BCE.
Sulla's dictatorship in 82 BCE, and the year of Catiline's conspiracy and Cicero's consulship (63 BCE).

The first triumvirate in 60 BCE, Caesar's consulship in 59 BCE (OpenStax line 88 says 60 BCE, which is likely a slip), the Ides of March 44 BCE, Philippi in 42 BCE, Actium on 2 September 31 BCE and the settlement of January 27 BCE.

OpenStax date slips to avoid: Spartacus's rising in 76 BCE (usually 73), Marius's five consulships as 105 to 101 BCE (usually 104 to 100), Marius's seventh consulship in 87 BCE (usually 86), Crassus's death in 54 BCE (the invasion began in 54, his death is usually put in 53) and Octavian stepping down as a dictator in 27 BCE (the Res Gestae says he refused the dictatorship).
Augustus's birth in 63 BCE and that the tribunician years ran from June. Both are used only to check the Res Gestae's own counts.
Whether 'three minae' in Polybius equals the 300 denarii in Livy for ransom at Cannae.
That Plutarch relied on Sallust or on a common source for Catiline. The pack does not say, so lesson 10 treats the agreement as possibly not independent.

That the pack has no narrative of the Italian wars (Livy Books 4 to 20), no life of Crassus or Antony, no account of the civil wars between 44 and 31 BCE other than Plutarch's Cicero, the Res Gestae and the textbook, and no Cicero or Tacitus. Lessons 4 and 12 depend on the textbook for those stretches.
